items.item: tags are used for retaining important historical snapshots for auditing purposes

A snapshot and a branch answer different questions even though both version the same underlying lake: a snapshot/tag pins one state for reading, while a branch is a writable, isolated view for building a new derived state before it is validated and merged — this topic uses a snapshot for the training-set reproducibility claim and names the branch separately for the case where the derived dataset itself needs its own working area.

at.step: Reveal: a moving target vs. a pinned one

items.item: lakeFS's zero-copy branching and DVC's content-addressable cache solve the same underlying problem (avoid duplicating bytes that haven't changed) at two different granularities: lakeFS at the scale of an entire repository's object set, DVC at the scale of one file — which is exactly why the decision in this topic is a scale question, not a feature comparison.

MLflow's LoggedModel searchability by dataset (this topic's claim) only has teeth if the dataset identifier logged against a run is itself a stable, content-derived digest rather than a mutable name — otherwise two different dataset states could share a logged name and the search would silently conflate them, which is why this topic pairs the tracker with the earlier reveals rather than teaching it standalone.

items.item: Label-version drift is easy to mistake for a data-quality bug because the symptom looks identical to data drift from the outside (the trained model's behavior shifts) — the diagnostic difference is that the *features* are provably unchanged (same snapshot, same hash) while only the label's own definition moved, which is why pinning the dataset alone is necessary but not sufficient for reproducibility.

A table-format tag (Iceberg) and a lakeFS tag serve the identical conceptual role — naming one immutable point in a changing dataset's history — at two different layers of the stack (one inside a single table's own metadata, one across a whole repository of many tables and files), which is why a team might reasonably use both at once rather than choosing one over the other.

The hook's six-month-old irreproducible dataset is not a hypothetical edge case but the default outcome of querying "the current table" with no snapshot at all — reproducibility failures of this kind are silent by construction, since the query itself never changes and nothing about running it again signals that its answer has.

DVC's MD5-based content hash is deliberately not a security mechanism (MD5's collision weaknesses would matter for an adversarial use case); its job is accidental-collision detection within one project's own files, a much weaker and sufficient requirement that the choice of hash function should be read against.

Reproducibility built on a snapshot is only as strong as the retention policy governing the snapshot itself — Iceberg's own documentation ties branch and tag lifecycles to explicit retention settings precisely because an unbounded number of pinned snapshots has its own storage cost, so 'reproducible' in practice means 'reproducible for as long as the policy keeps the pin alive,' not forever by default.

This topic's experiment-tracker reveal deliberately logs a dataset digest rather than a dataset name, because a name is exactly the kind of mutable reference the Hook's broken six-month-old dataset relied on — the tracker is only as trustworthy as the thing it links to, which is why it has to sit downstream of the snapshot/pin reveals rather than stand alone.

items.item: A lakeFS branch and a DVC pin both avoid duplicating unchanged bytes, but they fail differently under concurrent writers: a lakeFS branch isolates a whole derived dataset's writes from other branches until an explicit merge, while a DVC pin has no branching concept at all — two people editing the same file produce two different hashes with no automatic reconciliation, which is exactly why DVC is paired with Git's own branching rather than inventing its own.
